mexenone.text: Mexenone is an older benzophenone sunscreen filter, used to keep UV from damaging skin and so to slow sun-driven wrinkling and uneven tone. It is known more from dermatology allergy clinics than from current skincare routines, and its protective role is established chemistry rather than appearance trials.

gadusol.text: Gadusol is a natural UV-absorbing molecule from fish roe that researchers have explored as a bio-derived sunscreen ingredient. People interested in natural photoprotection cite it as a way to limit sun-driven skin aging; the evidence is lab and computational work, with no human appearance trials.

umbelliferone.text: Umbelliferone is a plant coumarin that absorbs UV light and is listed as a sunscreen agent, so it is mentioned as a way to limit sun damage that ages skin. Support for its use on skin comes from lab chemistry and animal work rather than human appearance studies.

padimate-a.text: Padimate A is a PABA-ester sunscreen filter related to the better-known padimate O, and it appears in discussions of historical sunscreen ingredients. Its role is UV protection that helps keep skin from sun-driven aging; it has little modern research and was never US-approved.

benzophenone-9.text: Benzophenone-9 is a water-soluble UV-absorbing compound that appears on lists of sunscreen ingredients, where the aim is limiting sun damage that ages skin. Published material is mostly environmental and analytical chemistry rather than studies of cosmetic benefit.

haa299.text: HAA299 is an experimental sunscreen filter designed to cover long-wave UVA-1 and the edge of visible light, wavelengths linked to skin aging and pigmentation. It has a small early study and an EU safety-committee opinion, with no long-term appearance trials.

acitretin.text: Acitretin is a prescription oral retinoid used for severe psoriasis and keratinisation disorders, so it is discussed in skin-appearance circles as a clinical retinoid option. Its evidence is in those medical conditions; use for cosmetic skin goals is off the label and not studied.

etretinate.text: Etretinate is a withdrawn oral retinoid once prescribed for severe psoriasis, mentioned in skin forums as the predecessor of acitretin. Its effect on visible skin was studied in psoriasis and keratinisation disorders; cosmetic use is untested.

alitretinoin.text: Alitretinoin (9-cis-retinoic acid) is a prescription retinoid used orally for severe chronic hand eczema and as a gel for Kaposi's sarcoma lesions. It comes up in skin discussions as a retinoid with visible skin effects, supported by trials in those conditions rather than cosmetic use.

seletinoid-g.text: Seletinoid G is a lab-designed retinoid intended as a topical anti-aging ingredient that irritates less than tretinoin. It is aimed at aged and photoaged skin; the evidence is a tiny short human study plus skin-model work.

motretinide.text: Motretinide is an older topical retinoid that was used for acne and compared with benzoyl peroxide in a 1984 trial. It is mentioned mainly as a historical acne retinoid, with little modern literature.

tazarotenic-acid.text: Tazarotenic acid is the active form that prescription tazarotene converts into on the skin, and tazarotene is promoted by some users as a strong anti-aging retinoid. Photoaging evidence exists for tazarotene itself; the metabolite alone is not sold or studied for looks.

oleyl-adapalenate.text: Oleyl adapalenate (Adapinoid) is a cosmetic retinoid pro-drug of adapalene, positioned for photoaging with better tolerability than retinol. Evidence for that use is one small 2024 trial suggesting improved wrinkles compared with retinol.

liarozole.text: Liarozole is an investigational drug that raises the skin's own retinoic acid levels, and it was tested orally in psoriasis and ichthyosis. People interested in retinoid-style skin renewal cite it as a mechanism; cosmetic use has no evidence.

talarozole.text: Talarozole is an investigational retinoic-acid blocker developed for acne and psoriasis, raising retinoid signalling without supplying a retinoid. Development for skin use was discontinued, and cosmetic use is untested.

chain: Convert to retinol then retinoic acid
retinyl-esters.text: Retinyl esters such as palmitate, acetate and propionate are used in creams as milder, more stable alternatives to retinol and tretinoin for anti-aging. They are promoted for smoother texture and fewer lines; skin outcome evidence is thin.

retinyl-acetate.text: Retinyl acetate is a stable vitamin A ester that appears in some anti-aging skincare as a gentler retinol alternative. Users apply it for smoother, younger-looking skin; no appearance trials exist.

ceramide-eop.text: Ceramide EOP is a barrier lipid listed in repair moisturisers, used to keep skin hydrated and calm so it looks smoother. Ceramides generally are well studied for barrier function; little is published on this subtype specifically.

hydrolyzed-hyaluronic-acid.text: Hydrolyzed hyaluronic acid is hyaluronic acid cut into shorter chains and marketed for deeper hydration and a plumper look. Users apply it in serums; direct evidence for the low-weight form's effect on appearance is thin.

sodium-hyaluronate.text: Sodium hyaluronate is the salt form of hyaluronic acid found in most moisturisers and serums, used for a hydrated, dewy, plumper-looking skin surface. It is well established in medical products; direct data on topical looks effects are limited.

tetrahexyldecyl-ascorbate.text: Tetrahexyldecyl ascorbate is an oil-soluble vitamin C ester used in serums for brightening and anti-aging as a gentler alternative to L-ascorbic acid. Human data come from small product-level studies.

chain: Inhibits tyrosinase as vitamin C form
ethyl-ascorbic-acid.text: Ethyl ascorbic acid is a vitamin C derivative sold for brightening and anti-aging, used by people chasing an even, radiant complexion. It is supported by lab studies, with no controlled human trials found.

chain: Converts to vitamin C in skin
sodium-ascorbyl-phosphate.text: Sodium ascorbyl phosphate is a stable, water-soluble vitamin C derivative used in cosmetics mainly as an antioxidant, and people use it for brighter skin and acne marks. Formulation data are plentiful; human appearance outcomes are sparse.

chain: Converts to vitamin C in skin
magnesium-ascorbyl-phosphate.text: Magnesium ascorbyl phosphate is a stable vitamin C pro-drug found in brightening serums, used for even tone and a fresher look. It is common in products but thin on direct human trials.

superoxide-dismutase.text: Superoxide dismutase is an antioxidant enzyme added to anti-aging products on the idea that limiting oxidative stress keeps skin looking younger. It is biologically central, but its cosmetic effect on appearance is essentially unstudied.

ubiquinone-topical.text: Topical coenzyme Q10 is included in anti-aging creams, with reports of reduced photoaging and wrinkle depth. Skin penetration is a recognised hurdle, and direct wrinkle trials are scarce.

palmitoyl-tripeptide-1.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-1 is a collagen-signal peptide that is one half of Matrixyl 3000, used in serums for wrinkles and firmness. Evidence is mostly lab and permeation data.

palmitoyl-tetrapeptide-7.text: Palmitoyl tetrapeptide-7 (Rigin) is an anti-inflammatory signal peptide, the second peptide in Matrixyl 3000, used in anti-aging and sensitive-skin products. Little isolated human data exist.

matrixyl-3000.text: Matrixyl 3000 is Sederma's two-peptide blend found in many anti-wrinkle serums, promoted for smoother, firmer skin. There is little independent human data on the blend itself.

palmitoyl-tripeptide-5.text: Palmitoyl tripeptide-5 (Syn-Coll) is a collagen-signalling peptide in anti-wrinkle creams, serums and microneedle patches, promoted for firmness. Evidence is small-scale and from multi-ingredient products.
